records.title: PoC pilot: base-8k vs Hierarchical-only 64k vs Fraise 64/8 at 100M dense, 500M base tokens
records.summary: Compares the three proof-of-concept models (base-8k, Hierarchical-only 64k — the 64k transformer on the hierarchical tokenizer — and Fraise 64/8, 64k in and 8k out) with the same 99.2M-parameter transformer on the same 500M base tokens of FineWeb-Edu text, by held-out bits per byte (BPB), to see what reading a large hierarchical vocabulary costs or gains at equal text. The three imported runs put base-8k first (1.130), Hierarchical-only 64k second (1.194) and Fraise 64/8 third (1.233). One seed each, more optimizer steps for the hierarchical models, and two training faults later found in both transformer baselines mean this ranking overstates the cost of a 64k vocabulary; the pilot has not been re-run with the fixes.

variants.title: base-8k: 8k transformer (byte-level BPE bpe-8k)
variants.description: The baseline: a standard transformer reading and writing the 8,192-token byte-level BPE, batch 64 × 512 positions, AdamW 1e-3. It is the small-vocabulary conventional model Fraise 64/8 has to beat on quality per unit of compute. Local folder pilot-base-8k (MLflow name pilot-base).

variants.title: Hierarchical-only 64k: 64k transformer on the hierarchical tokenizer
variants.description: The same transformer reading and writing the 65,536-token hierarchical tokenizer (about 41% fewer positions per byte) with an independent embedding row per token, batch 32, AdamW 3e-3. Fraise 64/8 shares its input side and tokenizer, so the two differ only in how macros are embedded and how the next macro is predicted. Local folder pilot-hier-64k (MLflow name pilot-symmetric).

variants.title: Fraise 64/8: compositional 64k in, 8k out (32-d residuals, local decoder)
variants.description: Fraise 64/8: macro inputs composed from base-token embeddings plus a 32-dimensional learned residual, the same transformer over macro positions, and a 10.1M-parameter local decoder that predicts the next macro's base tokens and END. Batch 32, AdamW 3e-3, as for Hierarchical-only 64k. Local folder pilot-fraise-64-8 (MLflow name pilot-fraise).

records.protocol: Commit d0fc54e (run from the t3 worktree t3-0e6f556d; dirty). Models: configs/100m/{8k,64k,fraise}.json (d=768, 14 layers, 12x64 heads, SwiGLU 2048, context 512). Data: FineWeb-Edu sample-10BT in stream order, 500,000,000 base tokens per run, 1 epoch, shuffle_data true. base-8k: batch 64 (minibatch 32), AdamW 1e-3 (configs/pilot-base-8k.json). Hierarchical-only 64k and Fraise 64/8: batch 32, AdamW 3e-3 (configs/pilot-hier-64k.json). Muon 0.02, warmup 200, weight decay 0.01, clip 1.0, BF16 + torch.compile, seed 1337, one seed per variant. Validation every 2,000 steps on CPU over 262,144 base tokens of the 0.05 GB held-out FineWeb-Edu prefix. Compare on validation/bits_per_byte only: validation/loss is per macro for 64k models and per base token for base-8k, so it is not comparable across variants. Note the step-count confound (15,259 vs 17,896 optimizer steps). Runs are imported, not re-run under AblationKit; MLflow run names keep the old names (pilot-base, pilot-symmetric, pilot-fraise).
records.body:
## Why this comparison

The project's claim is that Fraise 64/8 gives a better tradeoff between language-model quality, global transformer computation, sequence and KV-cache length, and access to the text inside tokens than either conventional baseline. The pilot is the first comparison at a size where the models learn real language: the same 99.2M-parameter transformer (d = 768, 14 layers, context 512 positions) in all three, trained on identical text, with budgets counted in base tokens so that each model sees the same bytes whatever its tokenizer.

Bits per byte (BPB) is the summed negative log-likelihood of the held-out targets, in bits, divided by the UTF-8 bytes those targets cover:

$$
\mathrm{BPB} = \frac{1}{B \ln 2} \sum_{t} -\ln p(x_t \mid x_{<t})
$$

where $B$ is the number of bytes scored. Unlike a per-token loss it does not depend on the tokenizer, so it compares models with 8k and 64k vocabularies directly. Lower is better.

Validation loss is per macro for the 64k models and per base token for base-8k, so only BPB is compared across variants.

## Variants

| Variant | Model | Input / output vocabulary | Batch (steps) | AdamW | Final BPB |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | ---: |
| base-8k (baseline) | base-8k | 8k / 8k | 64 × 512 (15,259) | 1e-3 | 1.1302 |
| symmetric-64k | Hierarchical-only 64k | 64k / 64k, hierarchical tokenizer | 32 × 512 (17,896) | 3e-3 | 1.1940 |
| fraise | Fraise 64/8 | 64k / 8k | 32 × 512 (17,896) | 3e-3 | 1.2332 |

Fraise 64/8 adds a 10.1M-parameter dense local decoder to the shared transformer (109.3M dense in total). The learning rates are the best of the 38M sweep; the batch for the hierarchical models was a deliberate choice of the project owner, recorded as a decision.

## Reading the result

- All three runs were imported from their files, not re-run under AblationKit; they come from commit d0fc54e in a separate, dirty worktree.
- One seed per variant: seed variance is unmeasured. The pilot report's bootstrap intervals over a larger held-out set (13.5M tokens) cover sampling of the validation text only.
- The hierarchical models took 17% more optimizer steps at a smaller batch and a higher learning rate; at 38M parameters, doubling Hierarchical-only 64k's steps later made no difference.
- Both transformer baselines kept untied embeddings at N(0,1) and had no final LayerNorm. At 38M parameters, fixing both cut Hierarchical-only 64k's gap to base-8k from 0.152 to 0.085 BPB, and base-64k (a standard 64k BPE) closed it. Fraise 64/8 already normalises its state before its decoder, so the Fraise-against-baseline differences here are also confounded.
- The comparison is at equal text. At equal transformer compute (equal positions) the pilot report finds the answer not established, because the base-8k value would have to be read before its learning rate had annealed.

records.body:
## Why this comparison

The pilot needed a learning rate for each architecture, and the hierarchical-tokenizer models, with larger vocabularies and fewer optimizer steps at equal text, could not be assumed to share base-8k's. Muon updates the transformer's weight matrices and was fixed at 0.02; AdamW updates everything else (embeddings, output heads, Fraise 64/8's residuals and gates), so its rate is the one swept.

Bits per byte (BPB) is the summed negative log-likelihood of the held-out targets, in bits, divided by the UTF-8 bytes those targets cover:

$$
\mathrm{BPB} = \frac{1}{B \ln 2} \sum_{t} -\ln p(x_t \mid x_{<t})
$$

where $B$ is the number of bytes scored. Unlike a per-token loss it does not depend on the tokenizer, so it compares models with 8k and 64k vocabularies directly. Lower is better.

## Variants

Nine runs, three learning rates for each model. All at 38M dense parameters (d = 512, 12 layers, SwiGLU 1024), 50M FineWeb-Edu base tokens, batch 64 × 512 positions, warmup 50, seed 1337. At the same batch in positions the hierarchical-tokenizer models see about 56k base tokens per step against 32k, so they take 891 steps against 1,526.

| Model | AdamW 3e-3 | AdamW 1e-3 | AdamW 3e-4 |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| base-8k (1,526 steps) | 1.4127 | **1.4087** (baseline) | 1.4395 |
| Hierarchical-only 64k (891 steps) | **1.5602** | 1.5985 | 1.6944 |
| Fraise 64/8, 64k in, 8k out (891 steps) | **1.5408** | 1.5926 | 1.6795 |

## Reading the result

- One seed per run, so differences of a few thousandths (Fraise 64/8 against Hierarchical-only 64k at 1e-3, 0.006) may be noise.
- Both hierarchical-tokenizer models are best at the top of the grid; a higher rate was never tried.
- The minibatch differs between runs: 16 for the two 3e-3 transformer runs (started before the runner switched to 64) and for all three Fraise 64/8 runs (out of memory at 64), 64 for the others. A minibatch only splits the 64-sequence step into accumulated parts, so the results are comparable across it.
- All nine runs were imported from their files (commit d0fc54e, a separate worktree), not re-run under AblationKit. The gap audit later repeated two of them on newer code with the same seed: 1.4087 for base-8k at 1e-3 and 1.5609 for Hierarchical-only 64k at 3e-3.
- The base-8k and Hierarchical-only 64k runs kept untied embeddings at N(0,1) and had no final LayerNorm; with both fixed, Hierarchical-only 64k's gap to base-8k fell from 0.152 to 0.085 BPB. The hierarchical-tokenizer models' preferred rate may differ once those faults are fixed; it has not been re-swept.

records.title: base-8k vs Hierarchical-only 64k gap audit at 38M dense, 50M base tokens
records.summary: Compares base-8k with Hierarchical-only 64k (the 64k transformer on the hierarchical tokenizer) at 38M parameters and 50M base tokens of text, adding two candidate fixes one at a time (embedding initialisation with standard deviation 0.02, then a final LayerNorm), to find out why the 64k model trailed by 0.152 bits per byte (BPB). With both fixes the gap fell to 0.085; halving Hierarchical-only 64k's batch to double its optimizer steps changed nothing (1.4996 against 1.4990); and base-64k (a 64k transformer on a standard BPE) with both fixes scored 1.4045, matching base-8k (1.4077 to 1.4139), so the rest of the gap belongs to the hierarchical tokenizer. One seed per variant, at 38M parameters only.

Tests whether the 64k model trails because it takes fewer steps. Added after the study was created. Local folder gap-hier-64k-emb002-finalnorm-b32 (MLflow gap-sym-emb002-finalnorm-b32).

Separates the cost of a 64k vocabulary from the cost of the hierarchical tokenizer. Added after the study was created. Local folder gap-base-64k-emb002-finalnorm (MLflow gap-bpe64k-emb002-finalnorm).

Models: configs model-8k.json / model-64k.json (d=512, 12 layers, SwiGLU 1024, untied). Training: lr-sweep-38m protocol (configs sweep-{0.001,0.003}-mb16.json): 50M FineWeb-Edu base tokens, batch 64x512 positions, minibatch 16, Muon 0.02, warmup 50, wd 0.01, BF16 + compile, seed 1337, one seed. Validation once at the end on 262,144 held-out base tokens. Compare validation/bits_per_byte; the gap = Hierarchical-only 64k - base-8k for the same treatment. Exceptions: sym-emb002-finalnorm-b32 uses batch 32 (1,782 steps); bpe64k-emb002-finalnorm (base-64k) uses the standard 64k BPE tokenizer with budgets calibrated to the same text (38,849,560 training and 203,610 validation tokens of its own, 1,186 steps; validation covered 971,133 bytes against 971,115 for base-8k). Jobs ran concurrently (up to four at a time), so throughput is not comparable across runs. MLflow run names keep the old names (gap-base-*, gap-sym-*, gap-bpe64k-*); local folders are gap-base-8k-*, gap-hier-64k-*, gap-base-64k-*.
records.body:
## Why this comparison

In the 100M pilot and the 38M learning-rate sweep, Hierarchical-only 64k (the 64k transformer on the hierarchical tokenizer) trailed base-8k by a wide margin (0.152 BPB at 38M, 0.064 at 100M). A code audit of both training paths found no bug in the loss, masking, packing, schedule or evaluation, but two non-standard choices that could weigh more on a 64k vocabulary: untied input embeddings left at PyTorch's N(0,1) initialisation, and no final LayerNorm before the output head. This study adds each fix to both models and measures how the gap moves, then runs two controls: more optimizer steps for the 64k model, and a 64k vocabulary built by a standard tokenizer (base-64k).

Bits per byte (BPB) is the summed negative log-likelihood of the held-out targets, in bits, divided by the UTF-8 bytes those targets cover:

$$
\mathrm{BPB} = \frac{1}{B \ln 2} \sum_{t} -\ln p(x_t \mid x_{<t})
$$

where $B$ is the number of bytes scored. Unlike a per-token loss it does not depend on the tokenizer, so it compares models with 8k and 64k vocabularies directly. Lower is better.

The quantity tracked is the gap for the same treatment,

$$
\Delta = \mathrm{BPB}_{64\text{k}} - \mathrm{BPB}_{8\text{k}}
$$

## Variants

All runs: 38M dense parameters (d = 512, 12 layers, SwiGLU 1024, untied embeddings), 50M FineWeb-Edu base tokens of text, AdamW 1e-3 for base-8k and 3e-3 for the 64k models (the best rates of the earlier sweep), Muon 0.02, seed 1337.

| Variant | Model | Embedding init | Final LayerNorm | Batch (steps) | BPB |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | ---: |
| base-default (baseline) | base-8k | N(0,1) | no | 64 (1,526) | 1.4087 |
| sym-default | Hierarchical-only 64k | N(0,1) | no | 64 (891) | 1.5609 |
| base-emb002 | base-8k | std 0.02 | no | 64 (1,526) | 1.4077 |
| sym-emb002 | Hierarchical-only 64k | std 0.02 | no | 64 (891) | 1.5180 |
| base-emb002-finalnorm | base-8k | std 0.02 | yes | 64 (1,526) | 1.4139 |
| sym-emb002-finalnorm | Hierarchical-only 64k | std 0.02 | yes | 64 (891) | 1.4990 |
| sym-emb002-finalnorm-b32 | Hierarchical-only 64k | std 0.02 | yes | 32 (1,782) | 1.4996 |
| bpe64k-emb002-finalnorm | base-64k (standard BPE) | std 0.02 | yes | 64 (1,186) | 1.4045 |

The gap for each treatment: 0.152 with neither fix, 0.110 with the embedding fix, 0.085 with both, 0.086 with both at batch 32, and −0.009 for base-64k with both.

A "final LayerNorm only" variant was planned but never run and has been removed from the list, so the final norm's effect without the embedding fix is not measured.

## Reading the result

- One seed per variant. Differences under about 0.01 BPB, such as base-8k with and without the final norm (+0.006) or base-64k against base-8k (−0.009), are not resolved.
- The two original-settings runs repeat two imported sweep runs with the same seed and configuration on a later commit (with the new switches off): 1.4087 against 1.4087 for base-8k and 1.5609 against 1.5602 for Hierarchical-only 64k. That shows the opt-in code changes did not alter default training; it is not an estimate of seed noise.
- base-64k's BPE was trained on the same FineWeb-Edu slice as the hierarchical tokenizer, while the 8k tokenizer was trained on a broader mix (BabyLM, Cosmopedia and FineWeb-Edu), so the 64k BPE is more in-domain. Its budgets count its own tokens and were calibrated to cover the same text.
- Jobs ran up to four at a time on the same machine, so `tokens_per_second` is not comparable across runs.
- The full reading, with the attribution of the gap, is in the gap audit's final report.

records.title: Which level-2 (64k) tokenizer closes the hierarchical tokenizer's gap at 38M?
records.summary: Compared four level-2 (64k) tokenizers over the same 8k base tokens and text, all keeping cross-word macros, on Hierarchical-only 64k with both fixes at 38M, and three of them on Fraise 64/8. The whole-word-phrase curriculum (word-bounded BPE to 40,000 entries, then cross-word merges of whole words only) was best: 1.4635 / 1.4711 BPB at seeds 1337 / 2 against 1.4983 / 1.4983 for the current tokenizer, at the same compression. It also improved Fraise 64/8 from 1.5401 to 1.5226 (one seed). The unrestricted curriculum came close (1.4753, one seed; within seed noise of the winner). The greedy prefix-closed vocabulary, which removes boundary lookahead, was worse for both models (1.5253 and 1.5481). Seed noise reached 0.008 BPB.
records.protocol: Hierarchical-only 64k variants: the gap audit's runs with both fixes (`experiments/level2/configs/hier-64k-lr3e-3-emb002.json`, `model-64k-finalnorm.json`): 38M dense transformer (12 layers, d 512, untied 64k embedding and head), input embeddings std 0.02, final LayerNorm, Muon 0.02 / AdamW 3e-3, batch 64 (minibatch 16), 50M base tokens of FineWeb-Edu in one pass (the same text for every tokenizer, because budgets count base tokens), validated once at the end on 262,144 base tokens of the held-out prefix. Fraise 64/8 variants: the 38M sweep's best settings (`model-fraise-38m.json`, `fraise-lr3e-3.json`: AdamW 3e-3, minibatch 16, no fixes, which Fraise does not support). Seed 1337; the `-s2` variants use seed 2 (`SEED=2`), which varies initialisation only (one data source, so document order is fixed). Only the tokenizer changes; every tokenizer has 65,536 entries of at most 8 base tokens and is learned from the same 0.3 GB FineWeb-Edu slice as hierarchical-64k. hier-current and hier-greedy-cross ran on the workstation; the rest ran unattended on Colab L4s (BF16) through `experiments/level2/colab.sh` at commits ff3eb42 and 4b208a7 of branch `level2-tokenizers`, which also measures each tokenizer (`tok/*` metrics). Two Colab runs (hier-phrases40k, fraise-phrases40k) lost their final archive after validation had been collected. References outside the study: base-8k (gap-base-emb002-finalnorm), base-64k (gap-bpe64k-emb002-finalnorm). Known confounds: AdamW 3e-3 not re-tuned per tokenizer; GPU type differs between workstation and Colab; Fraise lacks the two fixes; fewer positions per byte also means fewer FLOPs (all four tokenizers compress within 2%).

variants.title: Hierarchical-only 64k on hierarchical-64k (rerun)
variants.description: The current cross-word hierarchical BPE, rerun at the current commit so the study's baseline shares its code with the other variants; should reproduce gap-hier-64k-emb002-finalnorm (MLflow gap-sym-emb002-finalnorm).

variants.title: Greedy longest match, prefix-closed, cross-word
variants.description: Every entry appends one base token to another entry; segmentation is longest match left to right, so a boundary depends only on the next base token. Tests whether removing lookahead alone, keeping cross-word macros, closes the gap.

variants.title: Curriculum: whole-word pieces to 40,000 entries, then cross-word
variants.description: Word-bounded BPE to 40,000 entries, then 25,536 free cross-word merges over those tokens (SuperBPE's recipe with an earlier transition, so about as many multi-word entries as the current tokenizer). Cross-word macros may still start or end inside a word.

variants.title: Curriculum restricted to whole-word phrases
variants.description: As hier-curriculum40k, but cross-word merges only join tokens that are whole words, so no macro starts or ends inside a word (BoundlessBPE's restriction). Against hier-curriculum40k it isolates the cost of word fragments in cross-word macros; against hier-current, of the whole recipe.

variants.title: Fraise 64/8 on hierarchical-64k (rerun)
variants.description: Fraise 64/8 at the sweep's best settings (AdamW 3e-3, batch 64, minibatch 16, no fixes), rerun at the current commit as the Fraise baseline (imported sweep run: sweep-fraise-0.003).

variants.title: Fraise 64/8 on the greedy cross-word tokenizer
variants.description: Same as fraise-current with the prefix-closed greedy tokenizer: its END decisions depend only on the next base token. Tests whether lookahead, which did not matter for Hierarchical-only 64k, matters for Fraise's local decoder.

variants.title: Word-bounded hierarchical BPE (not run)
variants.description: Declared at first, then dropped: macros are meant to cross words. The tokenizer exists (experiments/level2/tokenizers/wordbpe-64k.json); base-64k remains the word-bounded reference.

variants.title: Greedy word-bounded (not run)
variants.description: Dropped for the same reason as hier-wordbpe.

variants.title: Curriculum at 90% (not run)
variants.description: Replaced by hier-curriculum40k: at a 90% transition only 6.5k merges cross words, far fewer multi-word macros than the current tokenizer.

variants.title: Curriculum restricted to whole-word phrases, seed 2
variants.description: hier-phrases40k with seed 2: replicates the study's best tokenizer against hier-current-s2. The tokenizer is retrained in the job from the same text by the same deterministic procedure.

variants.title: Fraise 64/8 on the whole-word-phrase curriculum
variants.description: fraise-current with the study's best tokenizer for Hierarchical-only 64k (word-bounded BPE to 40,000 entries, then cross-word merges between whole words only), trained in the job. Tests whether that tokenizer's gain carries over to Fraise, the model the tokenizer is for.

variants.title: Hierarchical-only 64k on hierarchical-64k, seed 2
variants.description: hier-current with seed 2 instead of 1337, which varies initialisation only (one data source, so the document order is fixed). With hier-current it gives the project's first estimate of seed-to-seed noise at 38M, needed to read the 0.01–0.03 BPB differences between tokenizers.
